## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Mendel's laws of inheritance — monohybrid and dihybrid cross

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Gregor Mendel (1822–1884), a monk in Brno, bred garden peas (*Pisum sativum*) from 1856–1863 and published in 1866. Peas were the right organism: true-breeding varieties, seven clearly contrasting traits, short life cycle, large numbers of offspring, and easy self- plus cross-pollination. He counted thousands of offspring and used mathematics — the first quantitative study of heredity. His work was ignored until 1900, when Correns, de Vries and Tschermak rediscovered it.

**Concept flow — how Mendel built the two laws (study in this order)**

| Step | What Mendel did | Result | What it proved |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Grew true-breeding (pure) lines for 7 traits for 2 years | Every line bred true | A clean starting material |
| 2 | Crossed pure tall (TT) × pure dwarf (tt) — the P generation | All F₁ plants tall (Tt) | One trait can mask the other → dominance |
| 3 | Self-pollinated the F₁ — the F₂ generation | 787 tall : 277 dwarf ≈ 3 : 1 | The dwarf factor had not vanished, only hidden → segregation |
| 4 | Self-pollinated the F₂ tall plants | 1/3 bred true (TT), 2/3 split 3:1 (Tt) | Genotype ≠ phenotype — two kinds of tall plants |
| 5 | Crossed F₁ back to the recessive parent (test cross) | 1 tall : 1 dwarf | Confirms F₁ carries both factors |
| 6 | Crossed pure round-yellow × pure wrinkled-green (dihybrid) | F₁ all round-yellow | Dominance holds per trait |
| 7 | Self-pollinated the dihybrid F₁ | F₂ = 315:108:101:32 ≈ 9:3:3:1 | Traits assort independently → second law |
| 8 | Test-crossed the dihybrid F₁ | 1:1:1:1 | Four gamete types in equal numbers |

**Monohybrid vs dihybrid cross — classified side by side**

| Feature | Monohybrid cross | Dihybrid cross |
|---|---|---|
| Traits tracked | One pair of contrasting traits (height) | Two pairs (seed shape + seed colour) |
| Pure parents | TT × tt | RRYY × rryy |
| F₁ genotype | Tt | RrYy |
| F₁ gametes | T and t (2 types) | RY, Ry, rY, ry (4 types) |
| F₂ genotypic ratio | 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt | 1:2:1:2:4:2:1:2:1 (9 classes) |
| F₂ phenotypic ratio | 3 tall : 1 dwarf | 9 round-yellow : 3 round-green : 3 wrinkled-yellow : 1 wrinkled-green |
| Law demonstrated | Law of Segregation (dominance shows in the 3:1) | Law of Independent Assortment |
| Punnett square size | 2 × 2 | 4 × 4 |

**Ratios cheat sheet — what each number tells you**

| Ratio | Seen in | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 3 : 1 | Monohybrid F₂ phenotype | Complete dominance of one allele |
| 1 : 2 : 1 | Monohybrid F₂ genotype (or phenotype in incomplete dominance / codominance) | Heterozygote is a distinct class |
| 1 : 1 | Test cross of a monohybrid (Tt × tt) | Heterozygote identified |
| 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 | Dihybrid F₂ phenotype | Two independent genes, each dominant |
| 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 | Dihybrid test cross (RrYy × rryy) | Four gamete types in equal numbers |
| Deviation from 9:3:3:1 | Same cross with linkage | Genes are on the same chromosome |

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** A tall pea plant of unknown genotype is test-crossed with a dwarf plant (tt). The offspring are 58 tall and 54 dwarf. Because dwarf offspring (tt) can only receive a **t** from each parent, the unknown parent must have supplied **t** gametes — so it was **Tt** (heterozygous), not TT. A 1:1 test-cross result is the standard proof of heterozygosity. If all offspring had been tall, the parent would have been homozygous TT.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) State the three laws and give the ratio each is based on. (2) Why did Mendel succeed where others failed — pure lines, discrete traits, large numbers, counting, mathematics. (3) Define test cross and back cross and give the expected ratios. (4) Draw the monohybrid Punnett square and label genotype vs phenotype ratios. (5) A 9:3:3:1 ratio that shifts toward the parental combinations signals linkage, not a broken law.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Mendel's factors (genes) occur in pairs, separate cleanly during gamete formation (Law of Segregation — 3:1, 1:2:1), and pairs for different traits assort independently (Law of Independent Assortment — 9:3:3:1). Dominance hides recessive alleles in the phenotype but never destroys them. **Self-check:** can you reproduce the 2×2 and 4×4 grids from memory, and explain why the test cross is the single most useful cross in genetics?

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Monohybrid cross scaffold: TT × tt → all Tt (F1) → F2 3:1 (phenotype), 1:2:1 (genotype) — draw the Punnett square; the ratios ARE the marks.
Trick 2: Dihybrid: TtYy × TtYy → 9:3:3:1 — quote the law of independent assortment for the ratio; test cross with a double recessive gives 1:1:1:1.
Trick 3: Three laws in one line each: dominance (one allele masks), segregation (alleles separate in gametes), independent assortment (genes on different chromosomes assort freely).
Trick 4: Test cross identifies an unknown genotype: with a homozygous recessive, all-dominant offspring → parent homozygous; 1:1 → heterozygous.
